entry: Artificial satellite that relays radio signals between widely separated points on Earth. It carries a transponder that amplifies incoming signals and retransmits them, creating a channel between a transmitter and a receiver. Uses include [[Broadcasting|television]], [[Telephone|telephone]], radio, internet and military communication. Some satellites sit in [[Geostationary orbit]], about 22,236 miles (35,785 km) above the [[Equator]], where they appear stationary and ground dishes need not move; most others form constellations in [[Low Earth orbit]], where antennas must track them. Radio waves travel by line of sight and are obstructed by the curve of the Earth, so satellites relay signals around it. International regulations allocate frequency bands to limit interference. In October 1945, [[Arthur C. Clarke]] published an article describing geostationary relay satellites. The first artificial Earth satellite, [[Sputnik 1]], was launched by the [[Soviet Union]] on October 4, 1957.

headword: Communist Party of the Soviet Union
sort_key: communist party of the soviet union
entry: Ruling political party of the Soviet Union, whose main ideology was [[Marxism–Leninism]]. It was the sole governing party until 1990, when the Congress of People's Deputies ended its constitutional monopoly. The party descended from the [[Bolsheviks]] faction, which, led by [[Vladimir Lenin]], seized power in the [[October Revolution]] of 1917. It pursued state socialism and a command economy. Economic stagnation and the Cold War arms race weakened it, and [[Mikhail Gorbachev]]'s reforms, including multi-candidate elections, reduced its power. After a failed coup in August 1991, Russian president [[Boris Yeltsin]] banned the party on November 6, 1991.

Branch of algebra that studies [[Commutative ring|commutative rings]], their ideals and their modules. Originally known as ideal theory, it began with [[Richard Dedekind]]'s work on ideals, built on earlier work by Ernst Kummer and Leopold Kronecker. [[David Hilbert]] introduced the term ring, and [[Emmy Noether]] recast many results in terms of the ascending chain condition, now known as the Noetherian condition. Wolfgang Krull introduced localization, completion, regular local rings and Krull dimension. The subject is the main technical tool of [[Algebraic geometry]] and is closely related to [[Algebraic number theory]]. Examples of commutative rings include polynomial rings and rings of algebraic integers, including the ordinary [[Integer|integers]]. Krull's principal ideal theorem is widely considered the single most important foundational theorem in the field.

Property of a binary operation whose result is unchanged when its operands are swapped. Examples include 3 + 4 = 4 + 3 and 2 × 5 = 5 × 2. Addition and multiplication are commutative for [[Real number|real numbers]], [[Complex number|complex numbers]] and [[Integer|integers]], and in every [[Field (mathematics)|field]]. Union and intersection of sets are commutative, as are logical AND and OR. Subtraction and [[Division (mathematics)|division]] are not, since 3 − 5 ≠ 5 − 3 and 1 ÷ 2 ≠ 2 ÷ 1. [[Matrix multiplication]] of square matrices is generally noncommutative, as is [[Quaternion]] multiplication. The property was used implicitly for centuries before it was named in the 19th century. [[Euclid]] assumed it for multiplication in his *Elements*, and ancient Egyptians used it to simplify products.

[[Ring (mathematics)|Ring]] with commutative multiplication. The study of such rings is called [[Commutative algebra]]. Examples include the integers, written ℤ as an abbreviation of the German word Zahlen, and polynomial rings. Every [[Field (mathematics)|field]] is a commutative ring in which each nonzero element is invertible; the rational, real and complex numbers form fields. An element is a unit if it has a multiplicative inverse, and an integral domain has no nonzero zero divisors. Localization adds inverses for elements of a multiplicatively closed subset; the rational numbers are the localization of ℤ at all nonzero integers. Real- or complex-valued continuous functions on a topological space also form a commutative ring.

Archipelagic country of three main islands in the Indian Ocean, at the northern end of the [[Mozambique Channel]]. The main islands are Grande Comore, Anjouan and Mohéli. The capital and largest city is Moroni, on Grande Comore. Comoros proclaimed independence from [[France]] on July 6, 1975. Its official languages are Comorian, French and Arabic, and the population is predominantly Muslim, with [[Islam]] the official religion. It is the only [[Arab League]] member entirely in the Southern Hemisphere and a member of the [[African Union]]. Mayotte voted against independence in 1974 and remains a French overseas department; Comoros continues to claim it, with backing from the African Union and the United Nations. The country has experienced more than 20 coups or attempted coups. It ranks in the bottom quartile on the [[Human Development Index]]. With a population of 944,388, it is among the most densely populated countries in the world.

Digital [[Optical disc|optical disc]] format for audio and computer data. Co-developed by [[Philips]] and [[Sony]], the CD was first released in [[Japan]] in October 1982 and stores uncompressed stereo audio. Standard discs are 120 mm (4.7 in) across and hold up to 74 minutes of audio or about 650 MiB of data, later extended to 80 minutes or 700 MiB. By 1991 CDs had surpassed the phonograph record and [[Cassette tape|cassette tape]] in U.S. sales. By 2000 they held 92.3% of the U.S. music market. The rise of [[MP3]] files and streaming led to its decline from the mid-2000s.

Type of [[Topological space|topological space]] central to general topology and analysis. A space is compact if every open cover has a finite subcover, which lets it behave in many ways like a finite set. Every [[Continuous function|continuous]] real-valued function on a compact space attains a maximum and a minimum. For subsets of [[Euclidean space]], compactness is equivalent to being closed and bounded, by the Heine–Borel theorem. In metric spaces it has several equivalent formulations, including sequential compactness, but these can fail in more general spaces. The closed unit interval [0,1] is compact, while the open interval (0,1) is not. Maurice Fréchet introduced compactness in 1906; Pavel Alexandrov and Pavel Urysohn developed the open-cover definition now standard. Arbitrary products of compact spaces are compact, by Tychonoff's theorem.

Legal entity representing an association of persons with a shared objective, such as profit or social benefit. Depending on jurisdiction, companies may be [[Corporation|corporations]], [[Partnership|partnerships]], [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit organizations]], [[Bank|banks]] or educational institutions. Most share a separate legal personality, limited liability, transferable shares, investor ownership and a managerial hierarchy. Incorporated companies are created by state registration, and companies may form corporate groups of parent and subsidiary corporations. In 1776, [[Adam Smith]] wrote in *The Wealth of Nations* that managers of other people's money would not take as much care as owners. After the [[Wall Street crash of 1929]] and the [[Great Depression]], the [[New Deal]] securities laws of 1933 and 1934 created a Securities and Exchange Commission empowered to require disclosure of material information to investors.

Branch of [[Historical linguistics|historical linguistics]] concerned with comparing languages to establish their historical relatedness. Genetic relatedness implies a common origin, or proto-language. Comparative linguists construct language families and reconstruct proto-languages, prefixing an asterisk to any form not found in surviving texts. The fundamental technique compares phonological and [[Morphology (linguistics)|morphological]] systems, [[Syntax|syntax]] and the lexicon, using the comparative method, which developed through the 19th century. Reconstructions can predict unattested features: [[Ferdinand de Saussure]] proposed laryngeal consonants in [[Indo-European languages]], a hypothesis vindicated by the discovery of Hittite. The method is less effective for distant relationships. Statistical approaches such as lexicostatistics compare basic vocabulary to determine relatedness but cannot reconstruct a proto-language.

Comparison of [[Myth|myths]] from different cultures to identify shared themes and characteristics. Scholars have used it to trace the development of religions and cultures, to propose common origins for myths, and to support psychoanalytical theories. Anthropologist C. Scott Littleton defined it as the systematic comparison of myths and mythic themes from a wide variety of cultures. Particularists stress differences between myths, while comparativists stress similarities. Many 18th- and 19th-century scholars held that myths evolved from poetic descriptions of the sun's behavior, but modern scholars lean toward particularism. Linguistic comparison has been especially successful in Indo-European studies: [[Zeus]], the Roman [[Jupiter (god)|Jupiter]] and the Vedic sky-god Dyauṣ Pitṛ have linguistically identical names. E.J. Michael Witzel's historical approach finds a storyline from creation to the end of the world in northern mythologies of Eurasia and the Americas, but not in southern ones.

Branch of [[Religious studies|religious studies]] comparing the doctrines, practices and impacts of the world's religions. It examines fundamental concerns such as ethics, metaphysics and the nature and forms of salvation, and compares the origins and similarities of religions. A common geographical classification distinguishes Middle Eastern religions, including [[Abrahamic religions]], Indian religions, East Asian religions, African, American, Oceanic and classical Hellenistic religions. [[Al-Biruni]] and Ibn Hazm, of the [[Islamic Golden Age]], are considered the fathers of comparative religion. In the 19th century, social scientists including Max Müller and [[Émile Durkheim]] took strong interest in comparative religion. Nicholas de Lange argues that the discipline grew within Christian theology faculties and tends to force religions into a Christian pattern. [[Hinduism]] and Theravada [[Buddhism]] describe salvation as escaping the cycle of [[Reincarnation]] rather than eternal life after death.

Rivalry for a goal that cannot be shared, where one's gain is the other's loss. Competition, an example of which is a [[Zero-sum game]], can arise among organisms, individuals, and economic and social groups. Animals compete for water, food and mates, and among [[Human|humans]] rivalries over wealth, power, prestige and fame often arise once basic needs are met. Competition is a tenet of market economies, where firms compete for the same customers, and it is studied in [[Psychology]], [[Sociology]] and [[Anthropology]]. It is often considered the opposite of [[Cooperation]], but in practice the two are usually mixed. The philosopher R. G. Collingwood argued that both are essential to an economic system, since parties co-operate in competing. Optimal strategies are studied in [[Game theory]]. In nature, competition for resources is a major force in [[Natural selection]].

Interaction between organisms or species that share a limited resource, such as food, water or territory. Competition lowers the fitness of both participants, because each one's use of the resource reduces the amount left for the other. It affects [[Ecosystem|community]] structure, species diversity and [[Population (biology)|population]] dynamics. There are three mechanisms: interference, exploitation and apparent competition, the last involving a shared predator rather than a shared resource. Under the competitive exclusion principle, less suited species must adapt or die out, although exclusion is rarely found in natural ecosystems. In interference competition, organisms fight directly: large [[Aphid|aphids]] eject smaller ones from better feeding sites on cottonwood leaves, and male [[Red deer]] contest for mates during the rut. In exploitation competition, organisms draw on a shared resource so that it is depleted for others. [[Plant|Plants]] also compete through allelopathy, the production of biochemicals.

Economic scenario in which firms contend to obtain limited goods. In classical economic thought, competition spurs firms to develop new products, services and technologies, giving consumers greater selection; more selection generally lowers prices compared with a [[Monopoly]] or oligopoly. The level of competition depends on the number of firms, barriers to entry, information and resource availability. Competitiveness refers to the ability of a firm, sub-sector or [[Country]] to sell goods and services in a [[Market (economics)|market]] relative to others. Neoclassical theory describes perfect competition, with many insignificant firms selling identical products and having perfect information; such conditions are rarely if ever observed. Empirical studies associate heightened rivalry with greater [[Productivity]].

Water-based sport of individual or team races in which swimmers move through water using the whole body. Competitive swimming is one of the most popular [[Olympic Games|Olympic]] sports, with events in butterfly, backstroke, breaststroke, freestyle and individual medley, plus freestyle and medley relays. A medley relay has four swimmers, each using a different stroke in the order backstroke, breaststroke, butterfly and freestyle. Competition rules govern the form of each stroke and the permitted [[Swimsuit|swimsuits]], caps and jewelry. Competitive swimming emerged in England in the 1830s, and men's swimming entered the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. In 1875 Matthew Webb became the first person to swim the [[English Channel]], using breaststroke. In 1902 Richmond Cavill introduced freestyle to the Western world. The international federation FINA renamed itself World Aquatics in December 2022.

[[Software]] that translates code from one [[Programming language|programming language]] into another, usually to produce an executable program. The name is mainly used for programs that translate high-level code into a low-level language such as [[Assembly language|assembly language]], object code or machine code. A cross-compiler produces code for a different [[Central processing unit|CPU]] or [[Operating system|operating system]] than the one it runs on, and a bootstrap compiler is a temporary compiler used to build a better one. Related tools include decompilers, transpilers that translate between high-level languages, and compiler-compilers. Compilers typically perform preprocessing, lexical analysis, parsing, semantic analysis, optimization and machine-specific code generation. An interpreter executes code without converting it to machine code and generally runs more slowly than native code. In the late 1950s, the [[Fortran]] compiler was one of the first practical compilers.

Branch of mathematical analysis studying functions of a complex variable. Complex analysis primarily studies [[Holomorphic function|holomorphic functions]], which are complex differentiable. Unlike real differentiable functions, a holomorphic function is always infinitely differentiable and equal to the sum of its [[Taylor series]] near each point of its domain. Integrals over a contour depend only on how the contour winds around the function's singularities, which often simplifies proofs. The theory of several complex variables extends the subject to higher dimensions. The subject is used in [[Number theory]], [[Physics]] and [[Quantum mechanics]], and in nuclear, aerospace and electrical engineering. Major contributors include Euler, Gauss, Riemann, [[Augustin-Louis Cauchy|Cauchy]] and Weierstrass. Iterating holomorphic functions produces [[Fractal|fractals]], which brought renewed popularity through complex dynamics.

Stress-related mental disorder arising from prolonged or repeated trauma. The [[World Health Organization]] includes it in ICD-11, which took effect in 2022, as a category of [[Post-traumatic stress disorder|PTSD]] with three additional clusters: emotional dysregulation, negative self-beliefs such as [[Shame]] or guilt, and disturbances in self-organization. Symptoms include prolonged terror, worthlessness or helplessness, and distortions of identity. The American Psychiatric Association has not included it in its diagnostic manual. In children, chronic maltreatment or family violence can cause it.

Mixed [[Landform]] of related volcanic centers and their lava flows and pyroclastic rock. Complex volcanoes, also called compound volcanoes, form when the eruptive habit or principal vent shifts. A [[Stratovolcano]] may develop a large [[Caldera]] that later fills with lava domes. Though comparatively unusual, they are widespread in geologic history: metamorphosed [[Tuff]] in Precambrian rocks of northern [[New Mexico]] shows that caldera complexes have long been important. [[Yellowstone National Park]] sits on three partly covered caldera complexes.

Material made from two or more constituent materials with dissimilar properties. The constituents remain distinct in the finished structure, which distinguishes composites from mixtures and solid solutions. Usually a binding matrix holds a filler of particles or fibers. Examples include [[Concrete]], reinforced concrete and [[Masonry]] bound with cement, lime or mortar; plywood and glulam [[Wood]]; and fibreglass, in which small glass fibers are embedded in an [[Epoxy]] or [[Polyester]] [[Polymer]]. Composites can be less expensive, lighter, stronger or more durable than common materials. Advanced composites were first developed for [[Spacecraft]] and [[Aircraft]]. Wattle and daub may be the oldest composites, over 6,000 years old. Vitruvius described pozzolana-based concrete around 25 BC, and Egyptian death masks were made of linen or papyrus soaked in plaster.

Visual organ of [[Arthropod|arthropods]] such as [[Insect|insects]] and [[Crustacean|crustaceans]]. A compound eye may contain from a few dozen to over 30,000 ommatidia, each a small photoreception unit with its own lens and photoreceptor cells. The image combines inputs from ommatidia pointing in slightly different directions. Compared with single-aperture eyes, compound eyes have poor resolution but a very wide view angle and fast motion detection, and some detect polarization of light. The flicker rate lets [[Honey bee|honey bees]] respond to movement in 0.01 seconds, compared with 0.05 seconds for humans. Apposition eyes form multiple inverted images, while superposition eyes form a single erect image. The [[Mantis shrimp]] has the most advanced apposition eye. Long-bodied decapods such as [[Shrimp]], prawns, [[Crayfish]] and [[Lobster]] alone have reflecting superposition eyes, which use corner mirrors instead of lenses.

Branch of [[Mathematical logic]] concerned with computable functions and Turing degrees. Also called recursion theory, it originated in the 1930s with work by [[Kurt Gödel]], Alonzo Church, Rózsa Péter, [[Alan Turing]], Stephen Kleene and Emil Post. Turing's 1936 model, the [[Turing machine]], became the main formalization of computability, and the Church–Turing thesis holds that any function computed by an [[Algorithm|algorithm]] is computable in this sense. In 1936 Church and Turing independently showed that the Entscheidungsproblem is not effectively decidable. The [[Halting problem]] is undecidable: no algorithm can decide for every program and input whether it halts. In 1970 Yuri Matiyasevich proved a theorem implying that [[Diophantine equation|Diophantine]] problems such as Hilbert's tenth problem have no effective solution. The field also studies computably enumerable sets and relative computability. Its results inform [[Computer science]] topics such as formal languages.

Function whose value an [[Algorithm|algorithm]] can compute for every argument. Computable functions are the basic objects of study in [[Computability theory]]. Because the notion of algorithm lacks a precise definition, formal definitions refer to a specific model of computation. The major models, including [[Turing machine]]s, register machines, [[Lambda calculus]] and general recursive functions, define exactly the same class of computable functions. The Church–Turing thesis, which is unprovable, asserts that no notion of computability computes more. Effective computability does not imply efficiency: some functions require running times that grow exponentially with input length. [[Computational complexity theory]] studies functions that can be computed efficiently.

Branch of [[Theoretical computer science]] that classifies computational problems by the resources needed to solve them. Resources include time, storage, communication, circuit gates and the number of processors in [[Parallel computing]]. A problem is inherently difficult if its solution requires significant resources whatever algorithm is used. Complexity theory asks what can be solved with restricted resources, while [[Computability theory]] asks what can be solved at all. Analysis of algorithms studies the resources of one algorithm, whereas complexity theory considers all possible algorithms for a problem. Classes include P, NP and PSPACE. The [[P versus NP problem]], one of the [[Millennium Prize Problems]], asks whether every problem whose solution can be verified in polynomial time can also be solved in polynomial time. NP-complete problems, including the [[Travelling salesman problem|traveling salesman problem]], are as hard as the hardest problems in NP.
